title: Akanda Corp (Feb 2018 TCC) Tax Court of Canada Ruling
subject: TCC motion for an extension of time to serve a notice of objection or appeal in an SR&ED tax dispute.
summary: Akanda Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 TCC 35, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision in which Chief Justice Rossiter refused to extend time to set aside the default dismissal of the taxpayer's 2007–2010 appeals, finding prejudice to the Respondent and no reasonable explanation for delay; the Federal Court of Appeal set it aside in 2018 FCA 200.
metaDescription: Examine the February 2018 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Akanda Corp and its lessons for Canadian R&D tax credit claimants.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Case Identification and Procedural Posture

The decision handed down by the Tax Court of Canada on February 19, 2018, indexed in industry repositories as Akanda Corp and formally reported under the style of cause Akanda Innovation Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2018 TCC 35 (Court File Nos. 2015-5215(IT)G and 2016-217(IT)G), represents a critical precedent in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax litigation. Adjudicated by Chief Justice Eugene P. Rossiter under the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) (SOR/90-688a), the ruling addresses the intersection between substantive multi-year SR&ED tax credit disputes and the strict procedural and evidentiary obligations required to maintain an appeal before the Tax Court of Canada. The Tax Court's order was subsequently set aside by the Federal Court of Appeal on November 1, 2018, in Akanda Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2018 FCA 200 (per Justice Webb, Rennie and Laskin JJ.A. concurring), which allowed Akanda's appeal, held that the Tax Court had committed errors of law in its treatment of the extension-of-time application, and granted the extension of time; the Tax Court decision therefore stands today as a cautionary illustration of procedural default that must be read together with the appellate ruling.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Tax Authority's Challenge

The underlying substantive dispute originated from claims filed by the corporate taxpayer, Akanda Innovation Inc. (the "Appellant"), for SR&ED expenditures alongside related Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) spanning four consecutive taxation years: 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010. Following review of the claims by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister" or "Respondent") issued Notices of Reassessment in May and July 2013 disallowing the Appellant's claimed SR&ED expenditures and denying the associated ITCs across all four taxation years.

After contesting the reassessments at the CRA Appeals Branch level, the Appellant instituted appeals before the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure across two separate dockets: Docket 2015-5215(IT)G and Docket 2016-217(IT)G. From the outset, the Appellant's litigation governance exhibited structural vulnerabilities: the Notices of Appeal were apparently drafted in a short period of time by Barrett Tax Law, the service that drafted them terminated its work on the pleadings, the counsel looking after the file resigned from the firm, and, although the Notice of Appeal for the 2007, 2008 and 2009 taxation years was filed on November 18, 2015, the Notice of Appeal for the 2010 taxation year was not submitted on time, requiring an application for an extension of time, which the Court granted, with a Notice of Appeal being created from the application itself. As the consolidated proceedings progressed through pre-trial case management, the Tax Court issued a formal Order dated September 12, 2016, establishing binding deadlines for pre-trial litigation steps. Difficulties of communication with the firm acting for the Appellant resulted in the Appellant never serving its list of documents under the September 12, 2016 Order; apparently due to irreconcilable differences, the Appellant's counsel removed themselves as counsel of record on January 6, 2017, but filed a motion to amend the September 12, 2016 Order on January 12, 2017, which was granted by Order in January 2017 (dated January 18, 2017 and referred to elsewhere in the Reasons as January 19, 2017) on the condition that the Appellant inform the Court before February 10, 2017 of new counsel—a condition with which the Appellant did not comply.

Because the Appellant failed to inform the Court of new counsel as required by the January 2017 Order, a status hearing was held on March 7, 2017. Neither the Appellant's corporate officers nor its legal counsel attended the March 7, 2017 status hearing. In the Appellant's absence, counsel for the Respondent brought a motion pursuant to Rule 125(8) and Rule 140(1) of the General Procedure Rules to have the appeal dismissed, which the Court granted, entering default judgment dismissing the 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010 SR&ED appeals in their entirety. The Appellant did not apply to set aside the default dismissal within the thirty-day period prescribed by subsection 140(2); upon discovering that the appeal had been dismissed, it retained new counsel and brought a motion, determined on written submissions, pursuant to Rule 12 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) seeking an extension of time to apply under subsection 140(2) to set aside the March 7, 2017 dismissal judgment, as well as an order setting aside that judgment.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Akanda Innovation Inc. operates across two interlocking statutory regimes in Canadian tax law: the substantive SR&ED provisions of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), the "ITA") and the procedural mechanics of the Tax Court of Canada Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. T-2) and the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure).

At the substantive level, a Canadian taxpayer claiming SR&ED tax incentives must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which underpins every SR&ED reassessment issued by the Minister. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes. Only activities meeting this threshold—alongside enumerated direct support work such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research commensurate with the needs of the core experimental work—qualify for expenditure pool deductions under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and ITCs under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA. Furthermore, pursuant to subsection 230(1) of the ITA, claimants bear a strict statutory obligation to maintain books and records at their place of business in Canada in such form and containing such information as will enable the Minister to verify the eligibility of the scientific activities and the quantum of qualified expenditures.

At the procedural level, once the Minister reassesses a taxpayer to deny SR&ED expenditures and ITCs, the taxpayer bears the initial legal and evidentiary burden of demolishing the Minister's factual assumptions on a balance of probabilities before the Tax Court of Canada. Under the General Procedure, pre-trial discovery, document production, and status hearings are governed by rigorous statutory rules. Specifically, subsection 140(2) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) provides that the Court may set aside or vary, on such terms as are just, a judgment or order obtained against a party who failed to attend a hearing, a status hearing or a pre-hearing conference, on the application of that party, if the application is made within thirty days after the pronouncement of the judgment or order; under the principles from Klein v. Schile quoted in Farrow and applied by Chief Justice Rossiter, such an application should be made as soon as possible after the judgment comes to the applicant's knowledge and should be supported by an affidavit setting out the circumstances under which the default arose and disclosing a defence on the merits. Where a taxpayer misses that thirty-day window, Rule 12 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) empowers the Court to extend or abridge any period of time prescribed by the Rules, either before or after the expiration of the prescribed period.

In adjudicating the combined motion under Rule 12 and subsection 140(2), Chief Justice Rossiter in 2018 TCC 35 relied on the principles set out by Associate Chief Justice Bowman in Farrow v. R., 2003 TCC 885 (quoting Klein v. Schile, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 78) and on the contextual approach he had described in Izumi v. R., 2014 TCC 107, considering four criteria that correspond to the four-part test derived from Grewal and Canada (Attorney General) v. Larkman, 2012 FCA 204—a test which the Federal Court of Appeal subsequently applied expressly in 2018 FCA 200. Under this governing framework, a party seeking an extension of time to set aside a default judgment must establish that doing so serves the overarching interests of justice by addressing four distinct criteria: whether the applicant demonstrated a continuing intention to pursue the appeal, whether the appeal has some merit, whether the respondent suffers prejudice arising from the delay, and whether a reasonable explanation exists for the delay. While the strength of one factor may compensate for weakness in another, all factors are weighed holistically against the evidentiary record.
The Court's Final Holding

Chief Justice Rossiter dismissed Akanda Innovation Inc.'s motion upon written submissions. The Court found that the first two criteria favoured the Appellant—the Appellant appeared to have had a continued intention to pursue the appeal, and the appeal appeared to have some merit, a "very low threshold" satisfied because the original Notice of Appeal was clear as to the issues being pursued—but the Appellant failed to satisfy the remaining two limbs of the test. Specifically, the Court held that allowing the motion to succeed would likely disproportionately prejudice the Respondent because the Appellant had failed to carry out its fundamental discovery obligations, and that no reasonable explanation had been given for the delay: the Appellant's claimed reliance on a January 12, 2017 e-mail from former counsel was rejected because the e-mail did not say what the Appellant claimed, the Appellant had been receiving Tax Court correspondence—including the January 2017 Order requiring it to inform the Court of new counsel by February 10, 2017—and the e-mail's advice to retain new counsel was not heeded until after the March status hearing. Moreover, the Court emphasized that it is the Appellant's fundamental obligation to prosecute the appeal on a timely basis, which did not occur. Consequently, at the Tax Court level the default judgment stood, with no order as to costs; the Federal Court of Appeal subsequently allowed Akanda's appeal, set aside the Order, and granted the extension of time, leaving the application to set aside the default judgments to be addressed by the Tax Court.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the taxpayer's 2007–2010 SR&ED claims in Akanda Innovation Inc. v. The Queen illustrates a dual-layer collapse common in high-stakes Canadian R&D tax disputes: the May and July 2013 reassessments denying the SR&ED expenditures and related ITCs (the specific grounds for which are not recorded in the Reasons for Order), compounded by fatal procedural and evidentiary defaults during Tax Court General Procedure litigation.
Procedural Non-Compliance and Abandonment of Case Management Orders

The immediate legal catalyst for the dismissal of Akanda Innovation Inc.'s appeals was its failure to attend the status hearing on March 7, 2017, following its failure to inform the Court of new counsel by February 10, 2017 as required by the Court's January 2017 Order and its failure to ever serve its list of documents. Under the Tax Court of Canada's General Procedure, SR&ED appeals involving multiple taxation years require structured discovery, formal exchange of lists of documents under Rules 81 and 82, and strict adherence to status hearing directives under Rule 125. In Akanda, the Court had issued an Order on September 12, 2016, granting an extension of time to file the Appellant's list of documents and setting out a timetable for other pre-trial litigation milestones.

Difficulties of communication in relation to the firm acting for the Appellant resulted in the Appellant never serving the list of documents required under the September 12, 2016 Order. Apparently due to irreconcilable differences, the Appellant's counsel removed themselves as counsel of record on January 6, 2017, but filed a motion to amend the September 12, 2016 Order on January 12, 2017; that motion was granted by Order in January 2017, which also required the Appellant to inform the Court before February 10, 2017 of new counsel—a requirement with which the Appellant did not comply. When the Appellant failed to appear at the March 7, 2017 status hearing, the Court properly exercised its jurisdiction upon the Respondent's motion under Rule 125(8) and Rule 140(1) to dismiss the appeals. The Appellant did not apply within the thirty-day period under subsection 140(2); according to the Court, upon discovering that the appeal had been dismissed, the Appellant retained new counsel and initiated a motion to reinstate the appeal rather quickly, but it was nonetheless required to seek an extension of time under Rule 12 before any application to set aside the judgment could be considered.
Breakdown in Corporate Governance, Counsel Oversight, and the "Continuing Intention" Standard

In attempting to justify its default at the March 7, 2017 status hearing and its subsequent delay in bringing the subsection 140(2) application, the Appellant relied on email correspondence from its former legal counsel. In Canadian tax litigation, corporate taxpayers frequently attempt to satisfy the "reasonable explanation for the delay" and "continuing intention to pursue the appeal" criteria by attributing missed deadlines to communication breakdowns, negligence, or inaction by former legal representatives or external SR&ED consultants.

Chief Justice Rossiter's rejection of this excuse reflects the principle, stated in the Reasons for Order, that it is the Appellant's fundamental obligation to prosecute the appeal on a timely basis; it must be noted, however, that the Federal Court of Appeal in 2018 FCA 200 did not endorse the Tax Court's analysis but set it aside for errors of law, and that subsequent decisions such as Brigitte Gratl v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 9, and 3964191 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 FC 894, cite the Federal Court of Appeal's Akanda decision for the proposition that the four Grewal factors need not all be satisfied and that the overriding consideration is that the interests of justice be served. Notably, the Tax Court found that the Appellant's continued intention to pursue the appeal appeared to be satisfied despite its non-compliance: the lack of compliance was attributed to a lack of communication from counsel of record, a relatively high amount of money was at stake, and upon discovering the dismissal the Appellant retained new counsel and initiated a motion to reinstate the appeal rather quickly; the Court observed that the standard established by the case law is one of outright neglect or lack of interest, which did not appear to be present. Where, however, a taxpayer relies on correspondence from former counsel to explain its delay, the Court will test that explanation against what the correspondence actually says and against the Court's own correspondence received by the taxpayer: in Akanda, the January 12, 2017 e-mail never mentioned that the status issue had been resolved, but only that the judge could take up to two weeks to issue a decision and that the Appellant should for now proceed as though the Court had granted the request, and it also advised the Appellant to retain new counsel. Because the Appellant had been receiving Tax Court correspondence—including the January 2017 Order requiring it to name new counsel by February 10, 2017—and did not heed the advice to retain new counsel until after the March status hearing, the e-mail did not furnish a reasonable explanation for the delay.
Affidavit Deficiencies, Defective Pleadings, and the "Some Merit" Threshold

Under subsection 140(2) and Rule 12, Chief Justice Rossiter, citing the principles from Klein v. Schile adopted in Farrow, noted that an application to set aside a judgment should be made as soon as possible after the judgment comes to the applicant's knowledge and should be supported by an affidavit setting out the circumstances under which the default arose and disclosing a defence on the merits. In analyzing the second criterion of the four-part test, the Court observed that proving an appeal has "some merit" is a "very low threshold" and noted that the original Notice of Appeal can be examined to determine whether an arguable issue exists.

In Akanda itself, the Court found that the appeal did appear to have some merit, that the original Notice of Appeal was clear as to the issues the Appellant was pursuing, and that the Appellant appeared to have some support for its position; two further realities nonetheless deserve attention. First, the Appellant's original filings had been prepared under difficult circumstances: the Notices of Appeal were apparently drafted in a short period of time, the service that drafted them terminated its work on the pleadings, the counsel looking after the file at Barrett Tax Law resigned from the firm, and the Notice of Appeal for the 2010 taxation year was not submitted on time, requiring an application for an extension of time, which the Court granted, with a Notice of Appeal being created from the application itself. Second, satisfying the low merit threshold did not, in the Tax Court's analysis, offset the Appellant's failures on the prejudice and reasonable-explanation criteria. Under the governing appellate framework articulated in Canada (Attorney General) v. Larkman, 2012 FCA 204 (relying on Grewal), the four extension-of-time criteria do not operate in rigid silos; rather, "a strong case may counterbalance a less satisfactory justification for the delay". In an SR&ED dispute, if a taxpayer possesses overwhelming, contemporaneous technical and financial evidence proving its 2007–2010 activities satisfied subsection 248(1) and subsection 37(1) of the ITA, exhibiting that evidence within the supporting affidavit can tilt the "interests of justice" inquiry in the taxpayer's favour despite procedural missteps. Conversely, as the Tax Court's reasoning in Akanda illustrates, meeting the "very low threshold" of some merit will not by itself rescue a taxpayer where the Court finds prejudice to the Respondent and no reasonable explanation for the delay.
Substantive SR&ED Documentation Failures, Evidentiary Decay, and Prejudice to the Minister

A critical analytical dimension of Akanda Innovation Inc. lies in understanding the context of the Minister's May and July 2013 denial of the 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010 SR&ED claims (the grounds for which are not recorded in the Reasons for Order), why the Appellant stalled during the 2016–2017 General Procedure discovery timetable (which the Court attributed to difficulties of communication with the firm acting for the Appellant), and why Chief Justice Rossiter weighed the factor of "prejudice to the Respondent" against the Appellant (namely, because the Appellant had not carried out its discovery obligations).

In Canadian SR&ED tax law, the substantive eligibility of R&D projects is governed by the five foundational criteria established by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and consistently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal. First, there must be a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures available in the public domain or within the corporate knowledge base. Second, the person claiming to be doing SR&ED must formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the procedures adopted must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through structured experiment or analysis. Fourth, the process must result in a technological advancement—that is, an advancement in the general understanding of scientific relations or technology known to a skilled professional in the field. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, the procedures followed, and the results must be kept contemporaneously as the work progresses.

When the CRA reassesses four consecutive taxation years, as occurred with Akanda's 2007–2010 claims in the 2013 reassessments, blanket disallowances are, in practice, commonly driven by four interrelated substantive and evidentiary deficiencies. Primarily, taxpayers suffer from an absence of contemporaneous technical records, relying instead on retrospective technical narratives drafted by external consultants at the time of filing Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) without dated test logs, failed prototype data, or design iteration records generated during the 2007–2010 fiscal periods. Simultaneously, claimants frequently conflate commercial development with experimental development, failing to separate routine engineering, debugging, or commercial product customization from genuine technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. From a financial standpoint, claimants also fail to substantiate labour and subcontractor allocations under subsection 37(1); without contemporaneous time-tracking sheets linking specific employees' hours directly to eligible experimental hypotheses versus commercial operations, the CRA Financial Reviewer denies the claimed salary base and the prescribed proxy amount. Finally, claimants frequently fall foul of funded research and "contract payment" exclusions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, whereby, under subsection 127(18), a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for ITCs must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments received or receivable. Where a corporate claimant performs technical development under commercial client contracts without clearly demarcating intellectual property retention, financial risk, and non-reimbursed experimental scopes, the CRA characterizes client revenues as contract payments, grinding the eligible ITC pool down to nil.

When a taxpayer suffering from these underlying documentation deficits appeals a multi-year reassessment to the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure, the litigation inevitably encounters an evidentiary wall during pre-trial document discovery and pleading particularization. In Akanda, the Appellant was required in 2016 and 2017 to comply with Court-ordered pre-trial steps—including serving its list of documents—concerning SR&ED activities that allegedly took place between 2007 and 2010. Lacking organized contemporaneous documentation from nearly a decade earlier, appellants in this position struggle to answer undertakings, prepare Rule 81 and Rule 82 lists of documents, or draft legally compliant pleadings—although in Akanda itself the Court attributed the failure to serve the list of documents under the September 12, 2016 Order to difficulties of communication with the Appellant's counsel rather than to any documented evidentiary deficit.

Furthermore, the third prong of the Rule 12 and subsection 140(2) test—prejudice to the Respondent—was decided against the Appellant in Akanda because of the Appellant's failure to carry out its discovery obligations, which the Court described as a fundamental obligation in litigation. By February 2018, when Chief Justice Rossiter adjudicated the motion, up to eleven years had elapsed since the 2007 taxation year. In SR&ED litigation, where technical eligibility often turns on the oral testimony of project engineers and CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) supplementing contemporaneous records, multi-year litigation delays caused by an appellant's default severely prejudice the Minister's ability to cross-examine witnesses whose memories of 2007–2010 bench trials have faded or who have left the parties' employ.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each procedural, evidentiary, and substantive legal requirement implicated in Akanda Innovation Inc. v. The Queen (2018 TCC 35) and its underlying 2007–2010 SR&ED reassessments against the Appellant's specific failures and the governing standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: The Taxpayer's Failure in Akanda Innovation Inc.
The Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Timely Institution of Tax Court Appeal
Income Tax Act, s. 169(1) & s. 167; Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure)

The Notice of Appeal for the 2010 taxation year was not submitted on time, so that an application for an extension of time was required, which the Court granted with a Notice of Appeal being created from the application itself; the appeals proceeded under Dockets 2015-5215(IT)G and 2016-217(IT)G.

Strict statutory compliance is required to vest jurisdiction in the Tax Court of Canada; extensions require proof that the taxpayer could not act within the time limit and possessed a bona fide intention to appeal.
Compliance with Case Management Timetables & Status Hearings
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), Rule 125 & Court Order dated Sept. 12, 2016

Never served the list of documents required under the Court's Order dated September 12, 2016, owing to communication difficulties with counsel; failed to inform the Court of new counsel before February 10, 2017 as required by the Court's January 2017 Order; and completely failed to attend the status hearing on March 7, 2017.

Court orders setting litigation timetables are mandatory, not aspirational; where neither the Appellant nor its counsel attended the status hearing, the Court granted the Respondent's motion under Rule 125(8) and Rule 140(1) of the General Procedure Rules and dismissed the appeal.
Timely Application to Set Aside Default Judgment
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), s. 140(2) & Rule 12

Did not bring an application to set aside the March 7, 2017 dismissal judgment within the 30-day period under s. 140(2); upon discovering the dismissal, retained new counsel and moved to reinstate the appeal rather quickly, but was required to seek an extension of time under Rule 12.

Once the 30-day window in s. 140(2) expires, the applicant must first obtain an extension of time under Rule 12; the Court applied the principles from Farrow (quoting Klein v. Schile) and the contextual approach from Izumi, considering the four criteria of continuing intention, some merit, prejudice to the Respondent, and reasonable explanation for the delay.
Prong 1: Continuing Intention to Pursue the Appeal
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), Rule 12; Akanda Innovation Inc., 2018 TCC 35 / 2018 FCA 200

Did not comply with any of the discovery requirements, but the Court nonetheless found that the requirement of a continued intention to pursue the appeal appeared to be satisfied, attributing the non-compliance to a lack of communication from counsel of record.

The standard established by the case law is one of outright neglect or lack of interest; a relatively high amount of money at stake, and the prompt retention of new counsel and filing of a motion to reinstate the appeal upon discovering the dismissal, supported a continued intention.
Prong 2: Demonstrating "Some Merit" via Affidavit & Pleadings
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), Rule 12 & s. 140(2); Income Tax Act, ss. 37(1), 127(9), 248(1)

Submitted an affidavit and original Notices of Appeal challenging the 2013 disallowance of 2007–2010 SR&ED expenditures and ITCs; the Court found the original Notice of Appeal clear as to the issues and the Appellant to have some support for its position.

While "some merit" is a "very low threshold" assessable against the original Notice of Appeal and was satisfied here, meeting that threshold did not, in the Tax Court's analysis, counterbalance its findings on prejudice and the absence of a reasonable explanation for the delay.
Prong 3: Absence of Prejudice to the Respondent (Minister)
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), Rule 12 & s. 140(2)
Sought in 2017–2018 to revive dismissed SR&ED appeals relating to the 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010 taxation years (reassessed in May and July 2013) without having completed its discovery obligations.

The applicant must establish that the Respondent suffers no prejudice from the delay; the Court held that allowing the motion to succeed would likely disproportionately prejudice the Respondent due to the Appellant's failure to carry out its fundamental discovery obligations.
Prong 4: Reasonable Explanation for the Delay
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), Rule 12 & s. 140(2)
Relied on a January 12, 2017 e-mail from former legal counsel to excuse the failure to comply with the Court's Order, the missed status hearing, and the subsequent filing delay.

The e-mail did not say what the Appellant claimed—it stated only that the judge could take up to two weeks to issue a decision and that the Appellant should for now proceed as though the Court had granted the request—and it advised retaining new counsel; because the Appellant was receiving Tax Court correspondence, including the Order requiring it to name new counsel by February 10, 2017, no reasonable explanation for the delay was established.
Substantive SR&ED Eligibility & Contemporaneous Documentation
Income Tax Act, ss. 37(1), 127(5), 127(9), 230(1), 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839
Underlying 2007–2010 SR&ED claims reassessed in May and July 2013 to deny SR&ED expenditures and related ITCs; the Reasons for Order do not record the Minister's specific grounds for the denial.

The taxpayer bears the onus of demolishing the Minister's assumptions by proving technological uncertainty, systematic investigation via hypothesis testing, technological advancement, contemporaneous records, and absence of excluded contract payments.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the procedural and substantive lessons of Akanda Innovation Inc. v. The Queen (2018 TCC 35) into actionable legal and technical compliance protocols, the following two applied case studies examine Canadian enterprises confronting the exact combination of multi-year CRA audit disallowances, contemporaneous documentation deficits, contractual exclusions, and Tax Court General Procedure litigation risks identified in the ruling.
Case Study 1: Multi-Year Embedded Firmware & Industrial IoT Developer Facing Retrospective Disallowance and Tax Court General Procedure Default Risk
Industry Context and Fact Pattern

Vanguard Telemetry Corp. ("Vanguard"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Waterloo, Ontario, designs ruggedized edge-computing sensors and low-power mesh-networking firmware for subterranean mining operations. For its four consecutive taxation years spanning 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024, Vanguard claimed $3.4 million in qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and $1.19 million in refundable enhanced ITCs (at the 35% CCPC rate) under subsection 127(10.1).

Following a joint technical and financial review, the CRA issued Notices of Reassessment disallowing 100% of Vanguard's SR&ED expenditures and ITCs across all four taxation years—mirroring the four-year blanket reassessment issued against Akanda Innovation Inc. in May and July 2013. The CRA's disallowance rested on three cumulative grounds. First, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) concluded that optimizing packet transmission across subterranean nodes involved standard protocol configuration and routine engineering rather than overcoming a fundamental technological uncertainty in computer science or radio-frequency (RF) engineering under subsection 248(1). Second, Vanguard's Form T661 project descriptions were drafted retrospectively by an external contingency-fee consultant fourteen months after each fiscal year-end, with no dated hypothesis logs or bench-test failure records maintained contemporaneously under subsection 230(1). Third, Vanguard's litigation governance broke down after it retained a sole-practitioner tax litigator to file Notices of Appeal under the Tax Court of Canada General Procedure. Mirroring the procedural pitfalls in Akanda, the Notice of Appeal for Vanguard's fourth taxation year was not submitted on time due to an administrative oversight and required an application for an extension of time; in addition, the initial pleadings drafted by counsel failed to plead specific material facts demolishing the Minister's technical assumptions, requiring an amendment. Nine months after the Tax Court issued a scheduling Order setting deadlines for discovery and amendments, Vanguard's external counsel ceased communicating effectively, placing Vanguard in imminent danger of failing to comply with the Court Order, missing a mandatory status hearing, and suffering a default dismissal that can only be set aside under subsection 140(2) and, once the thirty-day period has lapsed, only after obtaining an extension of time under Rule 12.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Tax Court Litigation Docket Control

To prevent the fatal procedural default suffered in Akanda Innovation Inc., Vanguard must immediately overhaul its corporate tax dispute governance by implementing a dual-custody docket and statutory calendar protocol. Vanguard's Chief Financial Officer and General Counsel must establish an internal litigation docket tracking system independent of external counsel, recognizing that the Tax Court treats timely prosecution of the appeal as the appellant's own fundamental obligation and expects an appellant that receives Court correspondence to act on it, regardless of communication failures with counsel. Every statutory deadline—including the 90-day window to file a Notice of Appeal under subsection 169(1) of the ITA, deadlines for filing an extension of time to appeal under section 167 to cure the late-filed final taxation year before a status hearing occurs, and every pre-trial milestone embedded in a Tax Court scheduling Order—must be logged on an internal corporate compliance calendar with automated 60-day, 30-day, and 14-day executive escalations.

Rather than leaving the Court's direction to identify new counsel unanswered, as occurred in Akanda when the Appellant failed to inform the Court of new counsel before February 10, 2017, Vanguard must instruct new specialist tax litigation counsel to formally serve a Notice of Change of Counsel under Rule 31, contact Department of Justice (DOJ) counsel for the Respondent to negotiate a consensual revised timetable in writing under Rule 12(3), and ensure both lead counsel and a corporate officer attend any scheduled status hearing in person. Furthermore, should any deadline require a Rule 12 extension motion, Vanguard must prepare a comprehensive, sworn corporate affidavit setting out a chronological log of bi-weekly corporate follow-ups proving an uninterrupted continuing intention to pursue the appeals, documented institutional explanations for any delay that are consistent with the actual content of counsel's correspondence and of the Court's own correspondence, rather than a mischaracterized e-mail from former counsel as in Akanda, and attached contemporaneous technical exhibits demonstrating high substantive merit to counterbalance any procedural delay under the Larkman framework.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Architecture

To overcome the CRA's finding of routine engineering and satisfy the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion, Vanguard must restructure its technical documentation pipeline inside its existing software engineering environment (Jira, Git, and Confluence) by prohibiting retrospective narrative writing. At the inception of a technical bottleneck, the Lead Firmware Architect must open a dedicated SRED-UNCERTAINTY Epic in Jira. The Epic header must explicitly document the systemic technological baseline—for instance, demonstrating that standard IEEE 802.15.4 mesh routing tables fail when rock-strata multipath attenuation exceeds 40 dB at 2.4 GHz while constrained to a 50 mW intrinsic-safety power budget—and explain why publicly available protocols and standard engineering calculators cannot resolve this conflict.

Every subordinate Jira ticket and Git commit within the Epic must follow a rigid four-field schema generated contemporaneously as the work progresses. First, the engineer must record the specific hypothesis formulated, such as proposing that a predictive Kalman-filtered time-division multiplex slot allocation algorithm will reduce packet collision re-transmissions by 38% without increasing microcontroller wake-time beyond 4 ms per transmission cycle. Second, the ticket must specify the experimental configuration and boundary parameters. Third, the engineer must attach the empirical test results and telemetry output, including raw oscilloscope traces, packet-error-rate CSV logs, and memory dump files. Fourth, the record must conclude with an analytical conclusion and hypothesis modification explaining scientifically why the trial failed or succeeded and how the findings dictate the next experimental iteration.
Step 3: Contract Terms and Subcontractor Structuring

Because Vanguard engages specialized RF testing laboratories and third-party embedded C++ developers, it must reformulate its commercial contracts to prevent expenditure disallowances under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. All subcontractor agreements must incorporate explicit Canadian situs and Statement of Work (SOW) clauses mandating that 100% of the contracted experimental development and testing work is performed physically within Canada, thereby satisfying paragraph 37(1)(a) and avoiding foreign expenditure disallowances outside the narrow subsection 37(1.4) salary rules. Furthermore, subcontractor SOWs must strictly bifurcate eligible "directly undertaken" support tasks—covered under the eight enumerated categories in subsection 248(1), such as computer programming, mathematical analysis, and testing directly commensurate with the RF attenuation experiments—from excluded commercial tasks such as printed circuit board enclosure industrial design or regulatory certification testing. Subcontractor invoices must cross-reference the exact Jira SRED-UNCERTAINTY Epic ID and break down hours at the 80% arm's-length contract inclusion rate required under subsection 127(9).
Step 4: Experimentation and Financial Cost Tracking

To insulate the claim against CRA Financial Reviewer adjustments and avoid discovery paralysis during Tax Court litigation, Vanguard must implement bi-weekly contemporaneous time-sheet attestation alongside automated evidence archiving. Engineers must log hours daily against specific Jira SRED-UNCERTAINTY tickets rather than commercial production tickets, and every two weeks, both the engineer and the Vice President of Engineering must digitally sign a time-allocation ledger linking payroll hours to specific experimental hypotheses. At the close of each fiscal quarter, Vanguard's enterprise resource planning (ERP) and Jira systems must automatically compile a read-only SR&ED Audit and Litigation Binder containing the dated Git commit histories, test failure logs, payroll registers, and T4 summaries. If the Minister reassesses the claim years later, Vanguard can produce a fully indexed Rule 81 or Rule 82 List of Documents within 30 days of the close of pleadings, eliminating any risk of failing a Tax Court scheduling order or causing delay prejudice to the Respondent.
Case Study 2: Advanced Bioprocessing & Specialty Chemical Manufacturer Facing "Contract Payment" Exclusions, Routine Trial-and-Error Disallowance, and Evidentiary Decay
Industry Context and Fact Pattern

Boreal Biopolymers Inc. ("Boreal"), an advanced materials manufacturer operating facilities in Mississauga, Ontario, and Trois-Rivières, Québec, develops bio-based barrier coatings for industrial packaging. Across four consecutive taxation years (2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022), Boreal conducted shop-floor pilot trials to synthesize a lignin-derived dispersion capable of withstanding high-humidity steam sterilization without delamination. Boreal claimed $5.8 million in SR&ED expenditures—comprising chemical engineering salaries, pilot-line materials consumed, and third-party analytical testing—and $1.12 million in federal ITCs.

During a multi-year audit concluded four years after the initial filings, the CRA denied the entire four-year claim—mirroring the multi-year disallowance in Akanda Innovation Inc.—on two primary substantive grounds. First, two of Boreal's largest commercial packaging customers had signed Master Supply and Development Agreements (MSDAs) providing milestone payments during the pilot trials; the CRA determined that Boreal was performing SR&ED on behalf of its customers and characterized $4.2 million in customer receipts as "contract payments" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA and applied them under subsection 127(18) to reduce Boreal's qualified expenditures, eliminating Boreal's qualified expenditure pool. Second, for the remaining unfunded runs, the CRA RTA concluded that varying catalyst ratios and curing temperatures on the shop floor constituted routine empirical trial-and-error optimization rather than a systematic investigation governed by scientific hypotheses under subsection 248(1). By the time Boreal's appeals reached the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure, the lead polymer chemist who supervised the 2019 and 2020 trials had retired and relocated overseas, and shop-floor batch sheets were stored in unindexed paper boxes. Faced with a Court Order requiring the completion of discoveries and undertakings within 120 days, Boreal's management stalled, risking the exact sequence of scheduling non-compliance, status hearing default, and prejudice to the Minister flowing from unperformed discovery obligations that doomed the taxpayer's motion before the Tax Court in Akanda Innovation Inc..
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Project Governance and Pre-Litigation Evidentiary Preservation

To eliminate the risk of witness unavailability and evidentiary prejudice to the Minister over multi-year audit and litigation cycles, Boreal must institute mandatory SR&ED exit interviews and sworn technical declarations alongside early discovery indexing. Under a binding corporate governance rule, any key scientific or engineering personnel departing the company, whether by resignation or retirement, must complete a structured technical exit debrief prior to final clearance. During this debrief, the scientist reviews the contemporaneous project files for all open taxation years and executes a detailed, dated Technical Declaration summarizing the technological uncertainties encountered, hypotheses formulated, and experimental methodologies executed during their tenure.

Simultaneously, immediately upon receipt of a CRA Proposal Letter—and well before Notices of Reassessment or Tax Court Notices of Appeal are issued—Boreal's tax counsel must institute a formal Litigation Hold across all plant servers, laboratory information management systems (LIMS), and accounting databases. All batch records, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy outputs, and customer contracts must be digitized and indexed by taxation year and project number, ensuring immediate compliance with any future Tax Court General Procedure timetable Order and neutralizing any claim of delay prejudice by the Respondent.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Architecture

To prove that shop-floor pilot runs constitute a systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis under subsection 248(1) rather than routine trial-and-error, Boreal must enforce a formal Design of Experiments (DoE) protocol inside its LIMS database before any pilot-scale batch is scheduled on the shop floor. Each protocol must state a causal scientific hypothesis linking molecular structure to macroscopic failure—for example, hypothesizing that cross-linking unmodified kraft lignin with bio-epichlorohydrin above 120°C induces steric hindrance and phase separation due to secondary hydroxyl group competition, and that introducing a zinc-carboxylate catalyst at a controlled 0.5 mol% loading will selectively favour primary phenolic esterification and prevent steam-induced hydrolysis.

Each pilot run must then be logged in a quantitative variable control matrix tracking independent variables (catalyst molarity, shear rate, dwell temperature) against dependent analytical metrics (glass transition temperature via differential scanning calorimetry, water vapour transmission rate, and peel strength in N/25 mm). Crucially, every batch record must conclude with a written scientific analysis explaining how the empirical data confirms or refutes the initial reaction mechanism hypothesis, providing the exact contemporaneous evidence required to satisfy the Tax Court's standard of proof.
Step 3: Contract Terms and Mitigation of "Contract Payment" Exclusions under Subsection 127(9)

To prevent customer milestone payments from disqualifying Boreal's SR&ED expenditures as "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, Boreal must redraft its commercial templates to strictly bifurcate commercial supply contracts from internal R&D. Hybrid "Master Supply and Development Agreements" must be replaced with pure Commercial Supply Agreements for Finished Goods conditioned on performance specifications, wherein the customer contracts solely to purchase a specified volume of coated roll-stock meeting a target moisture-barrier threshold at a fixed unit price upon commercial validation.

Each commercial agreement must contain explicit legal covenants stipulating that the customer is contracting solely for the delivery of commercial packaging material and is not contracting for the performance of SR&ED on its behalf. Furthermore, the contract must vest 100% exclusive legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, chemical formulations, process parameters, and know-how in Boreal, preserve Boreal's complete technical autonomy over whether and how to conduct internal R&D, and make customer payments strictly contingent upon the delivery of conforming commercial goods so that 100% of the financial risk of experimental failure rests on Boreal.
Step 4: Experimentation and Shop-Floor Expenditure Tracking

To ensure accurate segregation of shop-floor pilot trials from commercial production under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, Boreal must deploy segregated ERP work orders for "materials consumed" versus "materials transformed." Under subsection 37(8) of the ITA, the cost of materials qualifies for SR&ED ITCs only if the materials are consumed (rendered virtually valueless or scrapped as a result of the experimental process) or transformed (incorporated into a prototype that is eventually destroyed or holds negligible salvage value). Boreal must configure its ERP system to issue distinct SRED-PILOT work orders for experimental runs, tracking every kilogram of raw biopolymer resin and chemical reagent drawn under the work order through to a signed Scrap and Destruction Certificate—supported by weigh-scale tickets from the waste-disposal contractor—confirming the experimental batch was destroyed after destructive laboratory testing and never sold commercially. Finally, when commercial production lines are temporarily halted to run experimental trials, shop-floor operators and chemical engineers must badge into the SRED-PILOT work order via biometric shop-floor terminals, recording the exact start and stop timestamps of the experimental run, purge cycles, and post-trial decontamination to establish an unimpeachable contemporaneous audit trail for both CRA review and Tax Court litigation.
